text: to eliminate nasal carriage of staphylococci. Beta-haemolytic streptococci are also implicated in pyo- dermas including impetigo, erysipelas, and cellulitis. Necrotising fasciitis (p.180) may be caused by group A streptococci. Streptococcal infections continue to respond to phenoxymethylpenicillin or benzylpenicillin. Erythro- mycin is an alternative in patients unable to tolerate peni- cillins, but increasing resistance may be a problem;1 clin- damycin may be effective in patients with aggressive infections not responding to penicillin.3 Topical retapamu- lin is licensed for the treatment of impetigo due to either Staph. aureus or Str. pyogenes. For community-acquired mixed infections associated with necrotising fasciitis a combination of ampicillin-sulbactam, clindamycin, and ciprofloxacin has been advocated.2 Resistance is also emerging in Propionibacterium acnes; strains resistant to erythromycin, clindamycin, and tetracy- cline are reported to be common in patients after treatment for acne.1 Gram-negative bacteria are less frequently implicated in skin infections, but Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Proteus spp. can cause infections, especially if the skin is subjected to damp conditions. These organisms produce proteolytic enzymes that cause the resulting skin damage. Ps. aerugi- nosa may colonise burns and skin ulcers. Pseudomonal in- fections are treated with aminoglycosides and the anti- pseudomonal penicillins. Anaerobic organisms may colonise wounds, particularly chronic ulcers and fungating tumours. Topical metronida- zole has been used to control the offensive odour caused by these infections. 1. Espersen F. Resistance to antibiotics used in dermatological practice.
